card: The oxygen a sample will consume in five days — the standard measure of organic pollution.

frame.alt: Students standing at the edge of the Yamuna beside a line of foam on the water

answer: Biochemical oxygen demand is the amount of oxygen that micro-organisms will consume while breaking down the organic matter in a water sample, measured over five days at 20°C and reported in milligrams per litre. It is the standard proxy for organic pollution — mostly sewage. India's bathing-water criterion is less than 3.0 mg/L. Delhi's Yamuna stations report maxima between 46 and 72 mg/L.
explainHead: A measurement that takes five days
explainLead: BOD is not read off an instrument. It is the difference between two readings taken five days apart.
explain: The test is deliberately simple. A sample is sealed, its dissolved oxygen measured, and it is incubated in the dark at 20°C for five days. The oxygen is measured again. The difference is the BOD — how much oxygen the biology in that sample needed. The five-day convention is written BOD₅ and it is what Indian criteria are set against.

It measures demand, not a substance. Sewage, food waste, dairy effluent and slaughterhouse discharge all produce a high BOD; so does a dead algal bloom. What they have in common is organic carbon that bacteria will consume, and the oxygen consumed is taken out of the river.

That is why BOD and dissolved oxygen are two readings of one process. A stretch with BOD in the tens of milligrams per litre will not hold oxygen, because the demand exceeds anything the surface can resupply.

defs.d: The five-day test at 20°C. The convention behind every Indian BOD criterion.
Chemical oxygen demand — a chemical oxidation test that measures everything oxidisable, not just what bacteria will eat. Always higher than BOD, and not interchangeable with it.
Concentration multiplied by flow. Two stretches with the same BOD can carry very different loads.

after: The criterion is under 3.0. The last figure in that table is over twenty times it. Both numbers are published by the same agency in the same document, which is the whole reason a reading is worth printing against its limit rather than on its own.

readHead: How to read a BOD figure
readLead: It is a five-day laboratory result, and it inherits every limitation of one.
measure: A high BOD is evidence of organic pollution and is not evidence of what produced it. Domestic sewage and food-industry effluent are indistinguishable in this number.

Grab samples are points in time. CPCB publishes a minimum and a maximum per station per year rather than a mean, which is more honest than an average would be — but neither figure tells you how often the river was at either.

Concentration is not load. A stretch where most of the flow has been abstracted can show a very high BOD while carrying less total organic matter than a larger, cleaner-looking river downstream. On the Delhi Yamuna both are bad, but the distinction matters when comparing cities.
cannot: It cannot tell you about anything inorganic — metals, nutrients, salts and pharmaceuticals are invisible to it.
It cannot be compared with COD. They measure different things and the ratio between them varies by effluent.
It cannot be measured continuously. There is no live BOD feed anywhere, for anyone: the test takes five days.
A single maximum does not describe a year. It describes the worst sample taken.
